entities/coca-cola.md:
## "Less white" training and the post-BLM corporate turn

[[erik-carlson|Erik Carlson]] cited Coca-Cola in his April 2023 essay "Get Woke, Go Broke" as an emblem of corporate behavior following the 2020 [[black-lives-matter|BLM]] riots, recalling that the company ran employee training aimed at helping staff be "less white."{n} Carlson argued that in a country roughly 85% white, the message conveyed to the overwhelming majority of Coca-Cola's own customer base was that those customers were the problem with American society.{n} He treated the episode as part of a broader pattern in which corporations, under [[esg|ESG]] pressure, alienated their core markets to satisfy a small constituency outside them — behavior he said made no logical or business sense.{n}
entities/bud-light.md:
## Sponsorship of a TikTok trans influencer (2023 commentary)

In his April 2023 essay "Get Woke, Go Broke," [[erik-carlson|Erik Carlson]] recounted telling his 13- and 15-year-old sons that the trans person famous on TikTok was now sponsored by Bud Light and Nike, and being met with "who?" and "why would you think we'd know who you are talking about?"{n} Carlson took his sons' indifference as evidence that such figures may have far less cultural reach than audiences are led to believe, and that mentally well young people raised in religiously conservative homes may be largely immune to the messaging.{n} He placed the sponsorship within the wider [[esg|ESG]] dynamic in which corporations upset the majority of their customer base to appease a tiny fraction of people who are not customers at all.{n}
entities/black-lives-matter.md:
## Corporate funding after the 2020 riots (Carlson analysis)

[[erik-carlson|Erik Carlson]] identified corporate support for BLM as the point at which he first vividly noticed the pattern he later called "get woke, go broke."{n} While inner cities were still burning from the BLM and [[antifa|Antifa]] riots of 2020, he wrote, corporations were sending billions of dollars to the BLM organization.{n} In Carlson's account none of those donations reached Black Americans; the money instead funded Joe Biden's presidential run, while several BLM executives bought houses in predominantly white neighborhoods.{n} He characterized BLM as a money-laundering operation created and used by the [[deep-state|deep state]] to advance an agenda of chaos, confusion and division.{n}
entities/vanguard-group.md:
## Role in ESG enforcement (2023 commentary)

[[erik-carlson|Erik Carlson]] named Vanguard, alongside [[blackrock|BlackRock]] and [[state-street|State Street]], as one of the investment giants whose funds a corporation can be barred from if it fails to satisfy [[esg|ESG]] scoring organizations such as the Soros-funded Human Rights Campaign.{n} Exclusion from these managers' ETFs and mutual funds, in his analysis, reduces the number of holders of a company's stock and thereby drives down its price and valuation — the mechanism by which ESG functions as corporate control rather than investor choice.{n}
entities/state-street.md:
## Role in ESG enforcement (2023 commentary)

In "Get Woke, Go Broke," [[erik-carlson|Erik Carlson]] listed State Street with [[blackrock|BlackRock]] and [[vanguard-group|Vanguard]] as the major investment companies whose funds exclude corporations that do not comply with [[esg|ESG]] demands.{n} Because inclusion in these firms' diversified vehicles determines how widely a stock is held, Carlson argued that the threat of exclusion gives the scoring bodies effective leverage over corporate conduct.{n}
entities/george-soros.md:
## Alleged funding of ESG scoring bodies

[[erik-carlson|Erik Carlson]] wrote in April 2023 that Soros-run and Soros-funded organizations such as the Human Rights Campaign create corporate credit scores "kind of like the CCP" and force corporations to comply or face the wrath of those politically motivated groups.{n} In his account, a company that does not toe the Soros line is barred from the funds of investment giants including [[blackrock|BlackRock]], [[vanguard-group|Vanguard]] and [[state-street|State Street]], making Soros-linked NGOs the enforcement arm of the [[esg|ESG]] system.{n}
entities/donald-trump.md:
## Fed–Treasury merger and the BlackRock appointment (Carlson commentary)

In his April 2023 essay "Get Woke, Go Broke," [[erik-carlson|Erik Carlson]] revisited the claim that while Trump was president he merged the [[federal-reserve|Federal Reserve]] with the [[us-department-of-the-treasury|US Treasury]], understood in that community as dissolving the corrupt Fed into the Treasury.{n} What Carlson found confusing was that Trump appointed [[blackrock|BlackRock]] and [[larry-fink|Larry Fink]] — in his view unambiguous members of the elite club — to administer the merger, raising the possibility that Trump was forcing the deep state to buy up soon-to-be-worthless government assets and thereby destroy itself.{n} Carlson separately described Trump as, in his opinion, the greatest president who has ever lived.{n}
entities/federal-reserve.md:
## Alleged merger with the Treasury under Trump

[[erik-carlson|Erik Carlson]] wrote in 2023 that [[donald-trump|Donald Trump]], while president, was said to have merged the Federal Reserve with the [[us-department-of-the-treasury|US Treasury]] — an act interpreted in Badlands commentary as dissolving the corrupt central bank into the Treasury and effectively ridding the world of the Fed.{n} Carlson noted the paradox that the administration of this merger was handed to [[blackrock|BlackRock]] and [[larry-fink|Larry Fink]], and framed the arrangement as a fifth-generation-warfare puzzle whose true intent he could not resolve.{n}
entities/badlands-media.md:
## "Get Woke, Go Broke" (April 17, 2023)

Badlands Media published [[erik-carlson|Erik Carlson]]'s essay "Get Woke, Go Broke" on April 17, 2023, an opinion piece arguing that [[esg|ESG]] scoring is used by a deep state "club" to control corporate behavior at the expense of shareholders and customers alike.{n} As with all of the outlet's contributor pieces, it carried the standard disclaimer that Badlands Media articles and features represent the opinions of the contributing authors and do not necessarily represent the views of Badlands Media itself, alongside the outlet's statement that its content will always be free and that its collective of citizen journalists aims to take back the narrative from the mainstream media.{n}
